title: Cell structure
summary: How microscopes reveal cells, the structures shared by all cells, and how prokaryotic, plant, animal and fungal cells differ, including atypical cells and how eukaryotic cells first arose.

keyterms.definition: How many times larger an image is than the actual object: magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
The ability to distinguish two close points as separate; electron microscopes have much higher resolution than light microscopes.
Electron microscopy technique in which a frozen specimen is cracked along planes such as the middle of membranes, revealing internal surfaces.
Electron microscopy of rapidly frozen samples, allowing the 3D structure of proteins and other molecules to be determined without fixing or staining.
Light microscopy technique using antibodies linked to fluorescent dyes to show where specific molecules are located in cells.
Cell with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; has a cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop and 70S ribosomes.
Cell with a nucleus enclosed by a double membrane and compartmentalised by membrane-bound organelles; has 80S ribosomes and a cytoskeleton.
Prokaryotes (and mitochondria and chloroplasts) have smaller 70S ribosomes; the cytoplasm of eukaryotes has larger 80S ribosomes.
Division of a eukaryotic cell into membrane-bound compartments so that different conditions and processes are kept separate.
Network of microtubules and microfilaments in eukaryotic cells that supports the cell and enables movement of the cell and its contents.
Eukaryotic cells departing from one nucleus per cell, e.g. no nucleus in red blood cells and sieve tubes; many nuclei in aseptate hyphae and skeletal muscle fibres.
Homeostasis, metabolism, nutrition, movement, excretion, growth, response to stimuli and reproduction; all carried out by a unicellular organism.
Origin of mitochondria from engulfed aerobic proteobacteria and of chloroplasts from engulfed cyanobacteria that survived and became organelles.
Development of specialised cell types by expressing different genes, although all cells have the same genome.
Organisation of an organism as many cooperating cells; evolved repeatedly and allows larger size and cell specialisation.

questions.prompt: A mitochondrion is 2 µm long. In an electron micrograph its image is 40 mm long. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Convert to the same units: 40 mm = 40 000 µm. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 40 000 ÷ 2 = × 20 000.

questions.statement: Electron microscopes have higher resolution than light microscopes because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.
questions.explanation: Resolution is limited by wavelength. The short wavelength of electron beams allows details such as ribosomes and membranes to be distinguished.
Rearranging magnification = image size ÷ actual size gives actual size = image size ÷ magnification.

questions.prompt: Match each microscopy technique to what it is used for.

pairs.right: Splitting membranes to reveal internal surfaces
Locating specific proteins with labelled antibodies
Making particular structures glow in light microscopy

questions.explanation: These developments extended microscopy: freeze fracture revealed membrane proteins, cryo-EM resolves molecular structures, and fluorescence shows where molecules are.

questions.prompt: Which structures are common to all cells?
questions.explanation: All cells have DNA as genetic material, cytoplasm (mostly water) and a plasma membrane made of lipids. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and mitochondria, and animal cells lack walls.

questions.statement: Electron microscopes can be used to view living cells in colour.
questions.explanation: Specimens must be in a vacuum and are usually fixed or frozen, so they are not living, and images are black and white (colour is added artificially).

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of immunofluorescence over ordinary staining in light microscopy?
options: It gives higher resolution than an electron microscope
It shows the location of one specific protein in the cell
questions.explanation: Antibodies bind only to their specific target molecule, so the fluorescent tag reveals exactly where that protein is. Resolution is still limited by light.

questions.prompt: Order these from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: A membrane is about 10 nm thick, a ribosome about 20–30 nm across, a prokaryotic cell about 1–5 µm and a typical eukaryotic cell about 10–100 µm.

questions.text: The ability to distinguish two close objects as separate is called ___.
questions.explanation: Magnifying beyond the resolution limit only enlarges blur; resolution determines how much detail can be seen.

questions.prompt: Why are cells described as the basic structural unit of all living organisms?
options: Because all organisms are composed of one or more cells
Because all cells contain a nucleus
Because cells are the smallest structures that contain proteins
Because all cells are the same size
questions.explanation: All living things are made of cells, the smallest units that can carry out all functions of life. Cells vary in size and many lack a nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in a prokaryotic cell such as Bacillus?
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have DNA not associated with histones, in a loop in the cytoplasm (nucleoid), and 70S ribosomes. They lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

questions.statement: Eukaryotic cells have 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm, while prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes.
questions.explanation: 70S ribosomes are smaller. The 70S ribosomes also found inside mitochondria and chloroplasts are evidence for endosymbiosis.

questions.prompt: Match each cell type to the main component of its cell wall.
questions.explanation: Plant walls are mainly cellulose and fungal walls mainly chitin; animal cells have no wall, only a plasma membrane.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of compartmentalization in eukaryotic cells?
options: It lets enzymes and substrates for a process be concentrated, and keeps incompatible processes separate
It removes the need for a plasma membrane
It allows DNA to be stored without proteins
questions.explanation: Membrane-bound organelles create separate environments, e.g. lysosomes keep digestive enzymes away from the cytoplasm, and enzymes can be concentrated where they are needed.

questions.text: Mammalian red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements are atypical because they have no ___.
questions.explanation: Red blood cells lose their nucleus to make more room for haemoglobin; sieve tube elements lose theirs to allow sap flow, relying on companion cells.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a multinucleate eukaryotic structure?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibres form by fusion of many cells and contain many nuclei; aseptate fungal hyphae are also multinucleate.

questions.statement: Large permanent vacuoles and chloroplasts are found in typical animal cells.
questions.explanation: Plant cells typically have chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Animal cells have no chloroplasts and only small, temporary vacuoles, but have centrioles.

questions.prompt: A unicellular organism such as Paramecium must carry out all functions of life. Which list is correct?
options: Homeostasis, metabolism, nutrition, movement, excretion, growth, response to stimuli, reproduction
questions.explanation: These eight functions of life are what one cell must perform when it is the whole organism. Not all organisms photosynthesise or undergo meiosis.

questions.text: Microtubules and microfilaments together form the ___ of eukaryotic cells.
questions.explanation: The cytoskeleton maintains cell shape and enables movement of the cell and of organelles and chromosomes within it. Prokaryotes lack a eukaryote-type cytoskeleton.

questions.prompt: In an electron micrograph, which structure would identify a cell as eukaryotic?
options: A nucleus with a double membrane containing pores
questions.explanation: A nuclear envelope (double membrane with nuclear pores) is only found in eukaryotes. Ribosomes, membranes and walls also occur in prokaryotes.

questions.prompt: According to endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria evolved from which organisms?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria arose from engulfed aerobic proteobacteria; chloroplasts from engulfed photosynthetic cyanobacteria.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of mitochondria and chloroplasts to why it supports endosymbiosis.

pairs.right: Inner membrane from bacterium, outer from engulfing
Like the DNA loop of prokaryotes

questions.explanation: These shared features with prokaryotes are evidence that these organelles were once free-living bacteria.

questions.statement: Mitochondria and chloroplasts can only be produced by division of existing mitochondria or chloroplasts.
questions.explanation: These organelles divide by a process like binary fission and cannot be made from scratch by the cell, which is consistent with them being descended from bacteria.

questions.text: Chloroplasts are thought to have evolved from engulfed ___.
questions.explanation: Photosynthetic cyanobacteria taken up by a eukaryotic cell that already had mitochondria became chloroplasts.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the endosymbiotic origin of plant cells.
items: An ancestral cell engulfs an aerobic proteobacterium
The bacterium survives and becomes a mitochondrion
A cell with mitochondria engulfs a cyanobacterium
questions.explanation: All eukaryotes have (or had) mitochondria, but only some have chloroplasts, so the mitochondrion endosymbiosis came first.

questions.prompt: Cells in a multicellular organism have the same genome but different structures. How does cell differentiation occur?
options: Cells lose the genes they do not need
Different cells receive different chromosomes during mitosis
Different genes are expressed in different cell types
Each cell type mutates its DNA differently
questions.explanation: Differentiation results from changes in gene expression triggered by signals during development; the genome itself is not altered.

questions.statement: Multicellularity evolved only once, in the common ancestor of animals.
questions.explanation: Multicellularity evolved independently many times, for example in animals, plants, fungi, and red and brown algae.

questions.prompt: Which is an advantage of multicellularity?
options: Larger body size and specialisation of cells for different functions
Cells no longer need to divide
Each cell can carry out every function of life alone
It eliminates the need for gene expression
questions.explanation: Multicellular organisms can grow larger and divide labour among differentiated cells and tissues, increasing efficiency.

questions.text: The development of specialised cells by changes in gene expression is called cell ___.
questions.explanation: Differentiation produces specialised tissues; division only produces more cells.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly suggests mitochondrial DNA came from bacteria?
options: Mitochondria are found in all eukaryotic cells
Mitochondrial DNA is naked and circular, resembling bacterial DNA rather than nuclear DNA
questions.explanation: Nuclear DNA is linear and associated with histones; mitochondrial DNA is small, circular and naked like a bacterial chromosome.
